s: Dionysus is associated with Lydia (fatherland)
q: Thence am I; Lydia was my fatherland.

s: Agave leads the Theban women (on Kithaeron)
q: The one Autonoë led, one Ino, one thine own Mother, Agâvê.

s: Autonoë leads the Theban women (one of three bands)
q: The one Autonoë led, one Ino, one thine own Mother, Agâvê.

s: Ino leads the Theban women (one of three bands)
q: The one Autonoë led, one Ino, one thine own Mother, Agâvê.

s: Semele is mother of Dionysus (divine maternity)
q: Be of good cheer! Lo, it is I, The Child of Zeus and Semelê.

s: Semele is associated with the Tomb of Semelê
q: Fire leaps upon the Tomb of Semelê.

s: Zeus is father of Dionysus (divine paternity)
q: Be of good cheer! Lo, it is I, The Child of Zeus and Semelê.

s: thyrsus is a sacred wand (instrument of Dionysian worship)
q: This is Dionysus' wand.

s: Dionysian worship are restricted to the Elect (not open to sinners)
q: That may none Reveal, nor know, save his Elect alone.

s: Dionysus has fatherland Lydia
q: Thence am I; Lydia was my fatherland.

s: the earthquake shakes Castle of Pentheus (divine manifestation)
q: An Earthquake suddenly shakes the pillars of the Castle.

s: the fire from heaven burns Semele (at her tomb)
q: Ah, saw ye, marked ye there the flame From Semelê's enhallowed sod Awakened? Yea, the Death that came Ablaze from heaven of old,

s: the attack on the villages is carried out by the Theban women (on Hysiae and Erythrae)
q: On Hysiae and Erythrae that lie nursed Amid Kithaeron's bowering rocks, they burst Destroying, as a foeman's army comes.

s: Dionysus reveals Their intent and use (to me)
q: Their intent and use Dionysus oped to me, the Child of Zeus.

s: Dionysus is sent by God (to those strange springs)
q: And the holy women back to those strange springs Returned, that God had sent them when the day Dawned, on the upper heights;

s: Dionysus possesses thyrsus (sacred wand)
q: This is Dionysus' wand.

s: Dionysus is associated with the clustered vine (giver of wine to humanity)
q: He who first made for man the clustered vine.

s: Dionysus is denied by Pentheus (blasphemously)
q: for this thy sin, lo, He Whom thou deniest cometh after thee For recompense.

s: Dionysus is a God
q: since Dionyse Is God, and thou but mortal.

s: Pentheus wears rich trailing robe (in his transformation)
q: Aye, and next? DIONYSUS The same red Robe, falling to thy feet; and on thine head A snood

s: Pentheus wears snood (in his transformation)
q: The same red Robe, falling to thy feet; and on thine head A snood.

s: Pentheus wears dappled fawn-skin (as a Bacchanal)
q: Surely; the dappled fawn-skin and the wand.

s: Pentheus carries thyrsus (in the guise of a Maenad)
q: In my right hand Is it, or thus, that I should bear the wand To be most like to them?

s: Pentheus undergoes Pentheus's transformation (into a woman and Bacchanal)
q: O eye that cravest sights thou must not see, O heart athirst for that which slakes not! Thee, Pentheus, I call; forth and be seen, in guise Of woman, Maenad, saint of Dionyse,

s: Pentheus's transformation is a Bacchic madness (mental condition)
q: like a Bacchanal, and strangely excited, a spirit of Bacchic madness overshadowing him

s: Pentheus undergoes Bacchic madness (after being dressed as a Bacchanal)
q: like a Bacchanal, and strangely excited, a spirit of Bacchic madness overshadowing him

s: Pentheus undergoes Pentheus's trial (as a divine ordeal)
q: Therefore thy trial awaiteth thee!--But on; With me into thine ambush shalt thou come Unscathed; then let another bear thee home!

s: Pentheus undergoes Pentheus's death (as the consequence of his spying)
q: the lion walketh to the net! He finds his Bacchae now, and sees and dies,

s: Dionysus is a true Son (divine identity)
q: God's true Son, Dionyse, in fulness God, Most fearful, yet to man most soft of mood.

s: Pentheus's death faces a doom so fell
q: Fell, fell art thou; and to a doom so fell Thou walkest, that thy name from South to North Shall shine, a sign for ever!

s: Bacchae is a women (followers of Dionysus)
q: Damsels, the lion walketh to the net! He finds his Bacchae now, and sees and dies,

s: Bacchae worships Dionysus (as saintly devotees)
q: Pentheus, I call; forth and be seen, in guise Of woman, Maenad, saint of Dionyse,

s: Maenads is a wild Maids of God (mountain worshippers)
q: Sprites of the maddened mind, To the wild Maids of God;

s: Maenads is possessed by God
q: Watching in woman's guise, The spy upon God's Possessed.

s: Agave is related to Pentheus (as his mother)
q: Reach thou forth Thine arms, Agâvê, now, and ye dark-browed Cadmeian sisters! Greet this prince so proud

s: Agave carries Pentheus (as part of his foretold punishment)
q: The Queen, my mother. DIONYSUS Marked of every eye. PENTHEUS For that I go! DIONYSUS Thou shalt be borne on high! PENTHEUS That were like pride! DIONYSUS Thy mother's hands shall share Thy carrying.

s: Thebes has Wall of Seven Gates
q: Yea; and mine eye Is bright! Yon sun shines twofold in the sky, Thebes twofold and the Wall of Seven Gates....

s: the long dances is desired by me (ever again)
q: Will they ever come to me, ever again, The long long dances, On through the dark till the dim stars wane?

s: Wisdom is a freedom from fear (as defined by the Chorus)
q: What else is Wisdom? What of man's endeavour Or God's high grace, so lovely and so great? To stand from fear set free, to breathe and wait;

s: Law is a eternal order (unchanging and nature-born)
q: The Law that abides and changes not, ages long, The Eternal and Nature-born--these things be strong?

s: Justice is a Wrath of the Lord (made visible against the impious)
q: Hither, for doom and deed! Hither with lifted sword, Justice, Wrath of the Lord, Come in our visible need!

s: Wrath of the Lord smites the throat (with lifted sword)
q: Hither with lifted sword, Justice, Wrath of the Lord, Come in our visible need! Smite till the throat shall bleed,

s: God's judgment waits for them that worship the Ruthless Will
q: On them that worship the Ruthless Will, On them that dream, doth His judgment wait.

s: the Spirit of God is a eternal law (strong and unchanging)
q: That the Spirit of God, whate'er it be, The Law that abides and changes not, ages long, The Eternal and Nature-born--these things be strong?

s: Dionysus has chosen Dionysus's Chosen (as divine followers)
q: He will not brook it, if thou fright His Chosen from the hills of their delight.

s: Pentheus is a mortal (in contrast with Dionysus)
q: since Dionyse Is God, and thou but mortal.

s: Pentheus is a king (of Thebes)
q: Forth through the Thebans' town! I am their king, Aye, their one Man, seeing I dare this thing!

s: Pentheus has mother His mother (His mother's gift)
q: His mother's gift!--So shall he learn and mark God's true Son, Dionyse, in fulness God,

s: Pentheus is related to Bacchae (as their hostile observer)
q: the lion walketh to the net! He finds his Bacchae now, and sees and dies,

s: Messenger reports death of Pentheus
q: Pentheus, my king, Echîon's son, is dead!

s: Agave experiences truth and recognition (after her Bacchic frenzy clears)
q: No; 'tis the head--O God!--of Pentheus, this!

s: Agave is exiled exile (with her sisters, away from Thebes)
q: Farewell, O home, O ancient tower! Lo, I am outcast from my bower, And leave ye for a worser lot.

s: Cadmus is a father of Agave
q: My father, a great boast is thine this hour. Thou hast begotten daughters, high in power

s: Cadmus is a grandfather of Pentheus (maternal grandfather)
q: O Child, my daughter's child! who heldest true My castle walls

s: Cadmus founds Thebes (as its founder)
q: I, the great Cadmus, who sowed the seed-rows of this state Of Thebes, and reaped the harvest wonderful.

s: Cadmus is married to Harmonia (his wife and divine bride)
q: For thou must change and be a Serpent Thing Strange, and beside thee she whom thou didst bring Of old to be thy bride from Heaven afar, Harmonia, daughter of the Lord of War.

s: Cadmus goes to barbarous men (far off)
q: Far off to barbarous men, A grey-haired wanderer, I must take my road.

s: Pentheus's body lies in the tangled woodland (afar)
q: His body lies afar. The precipice Hath part, and parts in many an interstice Lurk of the tangled woodland

s: Cadmus possesses Pentheus's body (brought on a bier)
q: Enter from the Mountain_ CADMUS, _with attendants, bearing the body of_ PENTHEUS _on a bier_.

s: Bacchic frenzy is possessed by Bacchios utterly
q: But she, with lips a-foam and eyes that run Like leaping fire, with thoughts that ne'er should be On earth, possessed by Bacchios utterly

s: Pentheus is a king (of Thebes)
q: Pentheus, my king, Echîon's son, is dead!

s: the tearing apart of Pentheus occurs at where the dogs tore Actaeon
q: In what place was it? His own house, or where? CADMUS Where the dogs tore Actaeon, even there.

s: Dionysus is a god (son of Zeus)
q: Thus speaketh Dionysus, Son confessed Of no man but of Zeus!

s: Dionysus is a son of Zeus (divine son)
q: Thus speaketh Dionysus, Son confessed Of no man but of Zeus!

s: Dionysian worship is obeyed by Leader (as the sole object of obedience)
q: None save Him I obey, Dionysus, Child of the Highest, Him I obey and adore!

s: Thebes is beggared of manhood (so forlorn)
q: And deem'st thou Thebes so beggared, so forlorn Of manhood

s: Pentheus is a son of Echion
q: Pentheus, my king, Echîon's son, is dead!

s: Theban citizens is invited to Dionysian worship (Come)
q: Ho, all ye men that round the citadel And shining towers of ancient Thêbê dwell, Come! Look upon this prize

s: Zeus is the father of Dionysus (as declared by Dionysus)
q: Thus speaketh Dionysus, Son confessed Of no man but of Zeus!

s: Pentheus is dead dead
q: Pentheus, my king, Echîon's son, is dead!

s: Pentheus is a son of Agave (born in Echion's house)
q: And what child in Echîon's house had birth? AGAVE Pentheus, of my love and his father's bred.

s: Agave has child Pentheus (of my love and his father's bred)
q: And what child in Echîon's house had birth? AGAVE Pentheus, of my love and his father's bred.

s: Agave participates in the hunt on Kithaeron (as a Bacchanal hunter)
q: He was young in the wildwood Without nets I caught him! Nay; look without fear on The Lion; I have ta'en him!

s: Agave kills Pentheus (in Bacchic frenzy on Kithaeron)
q: Who slew him?--How came I to hold this thing? CADMUS O cruel Truth, is this thine home-coming? AGAVE Answer! My heart is hanging on thy breath! CADMUS 'Twas thou.--Thou and thy sisters wrought his death.

s: Agave possesses Pentheus's head (carried on a wand after the killing)
q: And, ah, the head! Of all the rest, His mother hath it, pierced upon a wand, As one might pierce a lion's

Amphitryon is father of Hercules
q: Yet, O let not this Offend thine ear, old man, for thee, not Jove, I deem my real sire

s: Amphitryon is responsible for the burial of Hercules’ children (because Hercules is forbidden to perform it)
q: This office. Let their mother, e’en in death, Clasp to her breast, and in her arms sustain, Our wretched offspring, whom in evil hour I slew reluctant. But when thou with earth Hast covered them

s: Hercules is a hero (great benefactor and friend of mankind)
q: THE. Benefactor of mankind, And their great friend?

s: Hercules is father of children of Hercules (whose murder he committed in madness)
q: AMP. Them did my miserable son beget, And when begotten slay, this impious murder He dared to perpetrate.

s: Hercules is husband of Megara (whose bed she preserved inviolate)
q: Have not I slain thee too who didst preserve My bed inviolate, and o’er my house Long watch with patient care

s: Hercules suffers from frenzy (induced by venom from the hundred-headed hydra)
q: AMP. This frenzy seized him sprinkled with the venom, Which from the hundred-headed hydra flowed.

s: Hercules commits murder of Hercules’ children and Megara (in a state of madness)
q: But I at last, wretch that I am, this murder Did perpetrate, and my own children slay

s: Hercules is subject to Juno (because of his parentage)
q: But Jove (or some one who assumed the name Of Jove) begot me; hence to Juno’s hate Was I obnoxious

s: Hercules is son of Jove (as Hercules believes, though he doubts Jove’s identity)
q: But Jove (or some one who assumed the name Of Jove) begot me

s: Hercules is son of Amphitryon (in Hercules’ acknowledged filial relationship)
q: Yet, O let not this Offend thine ear, old man, for thee, not Jove, I deem my real sire

s: Theseus commands Athenian youths (armed squadron)
q: THE. An armed squadron of Athenian youths I hither bring, who near Asopus’ stream Are stationed to assist your son in battle.

s: Hercules performs the Labours of Hercules (many and arduous)
q: Of what avail were it, should I recount The various labours I endured

s: Hercules kills the Hydra (the hundred-headed monster)
q: How I despatched the hydra too, that monster With heads surrounded, branching out anew

s: Hercules captures Cerberus (bringing him from the underworld to the light)
q: And having suffered many toils beside, Went to the mansions of the dead, to bring Hell’s triple-headed dog into the realms Of light

s: Hercules is exiled from Thebes (because of the laws concerning pollution)
q: My fate is such That in my native Thebes I must not dwell

s: Hercules undergoes Hercules’ exile (after murdering his children)
q: from Thebes retire, Since thus the laws ordain

s: Hercules suffers from grief (for my slain children)
q: In this one enterprise; to Argos go And for your friend obtain the great reward Promised for dragging from the shades of hell That execrable hound: lest if by you Deserted, I through grief for my slain children Should come to some calamitous end

s: Hercules retains Hercules’ weapons (despite their association with the murders)
q: But stripping off those arms with which through Greece I have achieved full many glorious deeds, Shall I expose myself to those who hate me, And die ignobly? I must not abandon But keep them still

s: Hercules uses Hercules’ shield (in the battle where the Giants were slain)
q: AMP. My son, my valiant son, Inured to many toils, who in that war Where earth’s gigantic brood were slain, advanced Among the gods to the Phlegræan field Armed with his buckler.

s: Hercules is overwhelmed by suffering and misfortune (after the murder of his children)
q: To him who was called happy once, such change Is bitterness indeed

s: Hercules rejects suicide (choosing to endure life with firmness)
q: Although I am most wretched, yet I thought I might be charged with cowardice for leaving These realms of light. For he who bears not up ’Gainst adverse fortune, never can withstand The weapon of his foe. I am resolved To wait for death with firmness

s: Theseus is friend of Hercules (bound by friendship and gratitude)
q: THE. I with his griefs am come to sympathize; Uncover him. AMP. That garment from your eyes Remove, display your visage to the sun. It ill becomes my dignity to weep: Yet I a suppliant strive to touch your beard, Your knees, your hand, and shed these hoary tears.

s: children of Hercules are killed by Hercules (during Hercules’ madness)
q: AMP. Them did my miserable son beget, And when begotten slay, this impious murder He dared to perpetrate.

s: Juno causes Hercules’ madness (through divine hostility)
q: AMP. This frenzy seized him sprinkled with the venom, Which from the hundred-headed hydra flowed. THE. Such Juno’s wrath.

s: Juno hates Hercules (because Jove loved Alcmena)
q: Who can pray To such a goddess, who, with envy stung, Because Jove loved a woman, hath destroyed The benefactors of the Grecian realm

s: gods inflict suffering and misfortune (on mortals)
q: A noble mind sustains Without reluctance what the gods inflict

s: gods are described as not needing support (according to Hercules’ reasoning)
q: her. For a deity If he be truly such, can stand in need Of no support.

s: Athens offers refuge to Hercules (after his exile from Thebes)
q: from Thebes retire, Since thus the laws ordain; and follow me To Pallas’ city

s: Athens honors Hercules (after his death, with sacrifices and a tomb)
q: but after death, when to the shades Of Pluto thou descend’st, with sacrifice And with the sculptured tomb, shall Athens grace Thy memory

s: Thebes expels Hercules (under the laws of exile and pollution)
q: My fate is such That in my native Thebes I must not dwell

s: Hercules’ madness suffers from frenzy (induced by venom from the hundred-headed hydra)
q: AMP. This frenzy seized him sprinkled with the venom, Which from the hundred-headed hydra flowed.

s: Theseus receives those favours (at thy hands)
q: THE. I who erst received Those favours at thy hands, now pity thee.

s: friendship is valued by Hercules (as steadfast support in misfortune)
q: Whoe’er prefers Wealth or dominion to a steadfast friend, Judges amiss

s: purification from pollution is required for Hercules (before entering Athens)
q: when thy hands are there Cleansed from pollution

s: Theseus offers refuge to Hercules (in Athens after his exile)
q: from Thebes retire, Since thus the laws ordain; and follow me To Pallas’ city: when thy hands are there Cleansed from pollution, I to thee will give A palace, and with thee divide my wealth

s: Theseus offers Athens’ palace (to Hercules)
q: To Pallas’ city: when thy hands are there Cleansed from pollution, I to thee will give A palace, and with thee divide my wealth

s: Theseus possesses land granted to Theseus (throughout Athens’ realm)
q: For portions Of land are through the realm to me assigned: These, while thou liv’st henceforth shall by thy name Be called

s: Amphitryon is a father of Hercules (aged)
q: AMP. My son, my valiant son, Inured to many toils

s: Iolaus is a companion of Hercules
q: Ye perchance knew somewhat Of Iolaus, great Alcides’ comrade, A name not quite unnoticed by renown.

s: Demophoon is a son of Theseus
q: Theseus’ son, Renowned Demophoon.

s: Demophoon rules this realm (by lot)
q: In this region dwell Two sons of Theseus, I am told, by lot Who portion out this realm

s: Demophoon is a protector of the suppliants (in the name of Athens)
q: Therefore go thou back To Argos, and this message to Eurystheus Deliver; tell him too if there be aught Which ’gainst our guests he can allege, the laws Are open; but thou shalt not drag them hence.

s: Demophoon is related to children of Hercules (by kinship and ancestral obligation)
q: from Lysidice, Daughter of Pelops, did Alcmena spring, One common grandsire gave your grandame birth, And theirs; so near in blood are you to them

s: Eurystheus is a king of Mycene (Argive ruler)
q: Mycene’s king, Eurystheus

s: Eurystheus persecutes children of Hercules (after Hercules’ death)
q: Eurystheus strove Immediately to slay us

s: Eurystheus sends Copreus (to seize the children of Hercules)
q: Mycene’s king, Eurystheus, sends me hither To fetch these vagrants home

s: Hercules is a father of children of Hercules
q: These are the sons Of Hercules, O strangers, they, to you, And to your city, humble suppliants come.

s: Hercules is a son of Jove (through Alcmena)
q: Alcides was the son of thundering Jove And of Alcmena

s: Hercules rescues Theseus (from Pluto’s caves)
q: Hercules led back your sire.

s: Iolaus is a guardian of the children of Hercules (after Hercules’ death)
q: When I in peace at Argos might have dwelt, I singly shared the toils of Hercules, While he on earth remained; but now he dwells In heaven, I guard his children, though protection Be what I need myself.

s: children of Hercules is a exiled race of Hercules
q: But with the exiled race of Hercules A voluntary exile, I partake Their evil fortunes

s: children of Hercules are children of Hercules
q: These are the sons Of Hercules

s: children of Hercules are suppliants at altars of the gods (seeking assistance)
q: On reaching Marathon and the domain Subject to the same rulers, here we sit Before the altars of the gods, and sue For their assistance.

s: children of Hercules are pursued by Eurystheus (because of his hostility toward them)
q: Eurystheus deems it meet To add this wrong to former wrongs, he sends His heralds wheresoe’er he hears we settle, And claims and drives us forth from every land

s: children of Hercules are denied freedom in Athens (if threats prevail)
q: For neither Trachis, Nor is that city of Achaia here, Whence thou by boasting of the might of Argos In words like those which thou hast uttered now, These suppliants didst unjustly drive away Though seated at the altars. If thy threats Here too prevail, no longer shall we find Freedom, not e’en in Athens

s: Chorus of Athenian old men supports children of Hercules (as suppliants of the gods)
q: ’tis our duty to revere The suppliants of the gods: with forceful hand Shall no man drag thee from this holy spot

s: Argives are subjects of Eurystheus (inhabitants and forces of Argos)
q: The king himself, Eurystheus, is their chief

s: Argives are hostile to Athens (under Eurystheus’ command)
q: For we in vain at Argos should possess A band so numerous of heroic youths, If we chastised not your assuming pride.

s: Athenians protect children of Hercules (against Argive demands)
q: But tremble not lest any brutal hand Should from this hallowed altar force away You and the children.

s: Marathon is a city in the Athenian dominions
q: SCENE.—BEFORE THE ALTAR OF JUPITER, IN THE FORUM AT MARATHON, A CITY IN THE ATHENIAN DOMINIONS.

s: Athens has generous temper of its sons
q: but I know Full well the generous temper of its sons, And rather would they die. For to the brave Shame is a load which renders life most hateful.

s: Athens maintains freedom of Athens (against Argive domination)
q: for this city As an appendage to the Argive realm I hold not, but its freedom will maintain.

s: Mycenae is ruled by Eurystheus (as its king)
q: Mycene’s king, Eurystheus

s: supplication at the altar is made by children of Hercules (to obtain protection from their enemies)
q: These are the sons Of Hercules, O strangers, they, to you, And to your city, humble suppliants come.

s: Iolaus is exiled from Argos (after Hercules’ death)
q: For when their sire Forsook this nether world, Eurystheus strove Immediately to slay us; but I ’scaped From that oppressor’s fangs, and though to me Lost is my country, I have saved my life.

s: freedom of Athens is defended by Demophoon (against Argos)
q: for this city As an appendage to the Argive realm I hold not, but its freedom will maintain.

s: Iolaus travels with children of Hercules (as exiles seeking refuge)
q: But we poor vagabonds, from city fly To some fresh city, ever forced to change Our dwelling

s: Iolaus has sailed with Theseus (in the bark used by Iolaus and Theseus)
q: With Theseus in one bark I sailed, and bore Their father’s shield

s: Copreus serves Eurystheus (as emissary)
q: Mycene’s king, Eurystheus, sends me hither To fetch these vagrants home

s: Copreus is from Argos
q: I am an Argive

s: Demophoon rules here (not with boundless power like a barbarian king)
q: For I rule not here With boundless power, like a barbarian king;

s: Iolaus guards children of Hercules (as their surviving protector)
q: Instruct these boys in every branch of wisdom, And make them like yourself, they can attain No higher pitch; strive to protect them still

s: Iolaus has the will to act (but not the power)
q: Thou hast the will to act, but not the power.

s: Iolaus fought in Sparta (alongside Hercules)
q: when thou didst lay waste The Spartan realms with Hercules

s: Macaria is a daughter (of Hercules)
q: Thou art no spurious child, But from the godlike seed of Hercules, O daughter, dost indeed derive thy birth.

s: Macaria saves children of Hercules (by accepting death)
q: you behold, mature for bridal joys, Dying to save them.

s: Alcmena is a mother (of Hercules)
q: call, come forth, Alcmena, mother of a noble son

s: Alcmena is a mother of a noble son
q: Alcmena, mother of a noble son, And listen to these acceptable tidings

s: Demophoon rules Athens (as a constrained ruler)
q: For I rule not here With boundless power, like a barbarian king;

s: Alcmena is a aged woman (and defender of the children)
q: But if thou dare To touch the children, with two aged foes Ignobly wilt thou strive.

s: Hercules is a father (of the children of Hercules and Macaria)
q: from that father spring, whose name With pride I utter

s: Hercules has a godlike seed (through which Macaria descends)
q: But from the godlike seed of Hercules, O daughter, dost indeed derive thy birth.

s: Eurystheus is a king (of Argos)
q: With numerous squadrons, and its king Eurystheus, Myself beheld him.

s: Eurystheus leads Argives (against Athens)
q: Argos comes With numerous squadrons, and its king Eurystheus

s: Eurystheus seeks to murder children of Hercules (because they may avenge their father)
q: He wants to murder _these_: for to their foes The rising blossoms of a noble race, To whom the memory of their father’s wrongs Is present, must be dreadful

s: children of Hercules descend from Hercules (as his noble offspring)
q: for to their foes The rising blossoms of a noble race, To whom the memory of their father’s wrongs Is present

s: Argos sends numerous squadrons
q: Argos comes With numerous squadrons

s: Athens protects the foreign suppliants (at the risk of war with Argos)
q: Should we reject the suppliant’s claim Appalled by Argos’ haughty state.

s: gods determine fate and the Destinies (through divine responses and destiny)
q: In just proportion, as the gods ordain, Is bliss diffused through life’s short span, Or sorrow portioned out to man

s: the oracles requires some blooming maid (from a noble sire)
q: The king informs us, that the seers, whose voice Expounds the will of heaven, have signified No bull nor heifer, but some blooming maid Who from a noble sire derives her birth, Must be the victim

s: the seers interpret the oracles (concerning the required sacrifice)
q: Every prophet who expounds The oracles, convening, have I searched Into each sage response of ancient times

s: Athenian army is ready for Argive invasion of Athens (with its left wing formed)
q: They are apprized, And the left wing is formed.

s: Argives is ready for Argive invasion of Athens (near enough for its leader to be seen)
q: So near that we their leader can distinguish.

s: Argive invasion of Athens is decided by the sword
q: with the sword our contest will decide.

s: Macaria’s sacrifice is a voluntary offering (made by Macaria)
q: for myself, old man, Am ready, ere they doom me to be slain, And here stand forth a voluntary victim.

s: death is a cure (for mortal suffering according to the wise)
q: For by the wise hath death been ever deemed The most effectual cure for every ill.

s: glory and reputation in war honors Macaria (after her death)
q: The nymph goes forth to meet a noble death, Her brothers and this land to save, And fame, with tributary breath Shall sound her praises in the grave.

s: Chorus supports Athens (against Argos)
q: My house, my country, to maintain Against the ruthless spoiler’s pride

s: Demophoon refuses to sacrifice his daughter (to fulfill the oracle)
q: Zeal have I shown abundant in your cause, But will not slay my daughter, nor constrain Any Athenian citizen to make Such an abhorred oblation

s: Minerva protects Athens (as its guardian and queen)
q: Descend with venerable mien, O thou our guardian and our queen, For on thy fostering soil we stand

s: Jove aids the spear I brandish (resistless)
q: Resistless Jove shall aid the spear I brandish unappalled by fear

s: Demophoon refuses to sacrifice Athenian citizens (as human offerings)
q: But will not slay my daughter, nor constrain Any Athenian citizen to make Such an abhorred oblation

s: Demophoon prepares Athenian army (to repel Argos)
q: Already have I made Each preparation to repel their onset. The city is in arms

s: Demophoon seeks a solution (that saves Athens without public blame)
q: See thou to this, and think of some expedient, How ye and how this country may be saved, Without the citizens’ calumnious tongues My fame assailing.

s: Iolaus is a aged kinsman (of the children of Hercules)
q: But from these And from thy aged kinsman, if thou wish For aught, to me thy last behests address.

s: Iolaus is a comrade (of Hercules)
q: It is Eurystheus’ wish The rather to seize me, and to expose To infamy, because I was the comrade Of Hercules

s: Alcmena is a royal dame
q: O royal dame, the message that to you I bring, is both concise, and what reflects

s: Chorus is a choral group
q: To me the choral song is sweet, When the shrill flute and genial banquet meet

s: Chorus advises Alcmena (to release Eurystheus)
q: To you, Alcmena, A little wholesome counsel would I give, This captive monarch to release, since such The pleasure of the city.

s: Hyllus challenges Eurystheus (to single combat)
q: Therefore with me encounter hand to hand, And if thou slay me, seize and bear away The sons of Hercules; but if thou die, My palace and hereditary rank Permit me to enjoy.

s: Iolaus is a aged friend (of Alcmene)
q: And Iolaus too, My aged friend?

s: Iolaus undergoes Iolaus's rejuvenation (through divine favor)
q: Two stars ’bove Iolaus’ chariot stood, And overshadowed it with gloomy clouds, Which, by the wise ’tis said, were Hercules Your son, and blooming Hebe: from that mist Which veiled the skies, the chief grown young again

s: Iolaus captures Eurystheus (after the battle)
q: the chief grown young again, Displayed his vigorous arms, and near the rocks Of Scyron, seized Eurystheus in his car.

s: Eurystheus is related to thee (near in blood)
q: For I with much reluctance undertook This contest; near in blood am I to thee, And of that race whence sprung thy son Alcides.

s: Eurystheus is a Argive tyrant
q: Binding his hands with chains, he hither brings The Argive tyrant, a distinguished prize

s: Eurystheus is a captive
q: But they to you commanded me to lead This captive, wishing to delight your soul

s: Eurystheus is a suppliant (while seeking preservation of his life)
q: esteem me now A suppliant, and though wretched, still a king

s: Eurystheus gives oracle of Phoebus (to Athens concerning his posthumous role)
q: But on this city, since it spared my life Through pious reverence, and forbore to slay me, Will I bestow an ancient oracle Of Phœbus

s: Eurystheus becomes guardian of Athens (after death)
q: to you a friend And guardian of your city, shall I rest Beneath this soil for ever

s: Eurystheus is a foe of descendants of Hercules (after death)
q: but a foe To those who spring from this detested race When with their armies they invade this land

s: Hercules is a son of Alcmene
q: Which, by the wise ’tis said, were Hercules Your son, and blooming Hebe

s: Hercules is a god (dwelling with the gods after death)
q: In heavenly mansions with the blest, Thy son, O venerable dame, doth rest

s: Hercules is married to Hebe (in the heavens)
q: Them two, both sprung from Jove, O Hymen, thou hast graced.

s: Jove is the father of Hercules
q: Which, by the wise ’tis said, were Hercules Your son, and blooming Hebe

s: Jove is the father of Hebe
q: Them two, both sprung from Jove, O Hymen, thou hast graced.

s: Argives is a army (opposing Athens)
q: When, to each other in the field opposed, We had arranged both armies

s: Argives is defeated in Argive invasion of Athens (by the Athenian forces)
q: But in this language either chief his troops Encouraged: “O ye citizens of Athens, O ye who till the fruitful Argive field, Will ye not from your native land repel The foul disgrace?” But with our utmost efforts Scarce could we put to flight the Argive host.

s: children of Hercules are expelled from each Grecian state (as suppliants at the altars of the gods)
q: But thou, moreover, from each Grecian state Me and these children hast expelled, though seated As suppliants at the altars of the gods

s: Athens is a free city (unafraid of Eurystheus)
q: But thou here hast found Those who were men indeed, and a free city Which feared thee not.

s: Alcmena seeks revenge on Eurystheus (for his persecution of Hercules and his children)
q: But he shall die to sate my just revenge.

s: Athens spares Eurystheus (out of reverence for the gods)
q: This city hath discreetly spared my life, More influenced by its reverence for the gods Than by the hatred which to me it bears.

s: single combat is proposed by Hyllus (against Eurystheus)
q: Therefore with me encounter hand to hand

s: Iolaus's rejuvenation is granted by Hebe (for one day through divine intervention)
q: a prayer Addressed to blooming Hebe, and to Jove, That for that single day he might recover The pristine vigour of his youth

s: death of Eurystheus is intended by Alcmena (as revenge)
q: But he shall die to sate my just revenge.

s: laws of Greece forbid death of Eurystheus (after his capture alive in battle)
q: by the laws of Greece, If I now die, my blood will fix a stain Of lasting guilt on him who murders me

s: Alcmena is from native land
q: Think not, presumptuous wretch, that thou shalt live Again t’ expel me from my native land.

s: Servant is a messenger
q: O royal dame, the message that to you I bring, is both concise, and what reflects

s: Servant reports victory of Athenian army (in battle)
q: In fight have we prevailed, and trophies reared On which the armour of your foes is hung.

s: Servant requests freedom from Alcmena (as the reward for his tidings)
q: and, oh, set me free: for nought But truth should from ingenuous lips proceed.

s: Messenger leads Eurystheus (as a captive to Alcmene)
q: But they to you commanded me to lead This captive, wishing to delight your soul

s: Dolon is a Trojan spy (volunteer for the nocturnal spying mission)
q: DOL. For my native realm, Facing this danger, to the fleet of Greece I as a spy will go

s: Dolon undertakes the nocturnal spying mission (to reconnoitre the Greek fleet)
q: DOL. For my native realm, Facing this danger, to the fleet of Greece I as a spy will go; and when I’ve searched Into the progress of our foes, return

s: Dolon uses Dolon’s wolf disguise (for covert movement)
q: DOL. I to my back will fit the tawny hide Of a slain wolf, will muffle up my front With the beast’s hairy visage

s: Dolon’s wolf disguise is a wolf disguise (made from a slain wolf’s hide and visage)
q: DOL. I to my back will fit the tawny hide Of a slain wolf, will muffle up my front With the beast’s hairy visage

s: Dolon seeks Achilles’ steeds (as his reward for the mission)
q: DOL. Achilles’ steeds: for when I stake my life On Fortune’s die, ’twere reasonable to strive For such an object as deserves my toils.

s: Hector promises Achilles’ steeds (as a reward to Dolon)
q: I, who prompted thee To this emprise, will not bely thy hopes, But to adorn thy noble father’s house, On thee Achilles’ generous steeds bestow

s: Rhesus be son of Strymon
q: Such tidings to unfold; for a brave chief, Your friend, the leader of a numerous host, Marches to fight the battles of this realm. HEC. But from what country? SHEP. Thrace, and he is called The son of Strymon

s: Rhesus leads the Thracians (to aid Troy)
q: Such tidings to unfold; for a brave chief, Your friend, the leader of a numerous host, Marches to fight the battles of this realm

s: Rhesus is an ally of Troy (newly arrived military ally)
q: Such is th’ ally who comes On Troy’s behalf to combat

s: Rhesus is the son of Strymon
q: SHEP. Thrace, and he is called The son of Strymon.

s: Chorus of Trojan sentinels guard the camp
q: CHOR. We guard the camp.

s: Rhesus is the child of the Muse (through Strymon’s union with the Muse)
q: I. 2. Doth Strymon summon to the field: of yore When he the tuneful Muse addressed, A gliding stream he sought her snowy breast, Thee, lovely youth, the yielding goddess bore

s: Rhesus possesses the golden shield of Rhesus (ornamented with gold)
q: o’er his shoulders hung a shield Adorned with sculptures wrought in massive gold

s: the chariot of Rhesus be drawn by Achilles’ steeds (that browsed the Phthian lawn)
q: May he mount that chariot drawn By steeds that browsed the Phthian lawn When our brave lord, the Mars of Greece, hath slain

s: Achilles’ steeds are a immortal horses (of divine lineage)
q: HEC. Although thou in thy wishes to possess Those steeds hast interfered with me: for sprung From an immortal race themselves immortal They bear Pelides through the ranks of war

s: Achilles’ steeds belong to Achilles (given to Peleus by Neptune)
q: They bear Pelides through the ranks of war, Neptune, ’tis said, the king of ocean, tamed them And gave to Peleus

s: the shepherd bring Rhesus
q: SHEP. Most gracious monarch, may I ever greet My lords with tidings such as now I bring!

s: the shepherd comes from Ida (an inhabitant of its mountain region)
q: us rustics he alarmed, Who dwell on Ida’s mount, the ancient seat Of Ilion’s first inhabitants

s: the Greeks occupies Greek encampment (before Troy)
q: CHOR. All night long, O Hector, The Grecian camp hath kindled fires

s: Chorus of Trojan sentinels reports activity in Greek encampment (at night)
q: CHOR. All night long, O Hector, The Grecian camp hath kindled fires, the torches Amid their fleet are blazing

s: Greek encampment contains the Greek fleet (on the shore)
q: the torches Amid their fleet are blazing

s: the Greeks prepares for the Greek flight (as suspected by Hector)
q: these dastards hope They in their barks shall from this shore escape

s: the Greek fleet is protected by Achilles (against a Trojan attack)
q: The son of Peleus, from your flaming torches Who will protect the fleet, nor suffer you Utterly to destroy the Grecian host

s: Troy receives Rhesus (as a hospitable ally)
q: let Rhesus Refulgent in his golden arms draw near, For Ilion shall receive him as her friend

s: hospitality is offered to Rhesus (by Troy)
q: CHOR. Since he comes But as a guest, not partner in the war, Let him approach your hospitable board

s: Hector is a Trojan commander
q: Instantly therefore through the host proclaim These orders: “Take up arms, and rouse from sleep

s: Hector commands the Trojan army (in defense of Troy)
q: Instantly therefore through the host proclaim These orders: “Take up arms, and rouse from sleep

s: Hector commands the nocturnal spying mission (by seeking a spy for the Greek fleet)
q: HEC. What brave Trojan, present At this our conference, as a spy will go T’ explore the Grecian navy?

s: Hector prolong the successful battle (till I had burnt their ships)
q: Had not the sun withdrawn his radiant beams, I the successful battle had prolonged Till I had burnt their ships

s: Aeneas ask about the watch (by night)
q: ÆNE. What mean the watch, O Hector, who by night Were to their stations in the camp assigned, That they, with terror smitten, at your chamber In a nocturnal council have assembled?

s: Aeneas advises Hector (against a premature night attack)
q: Our troops Let us then leave to rest from martial toils, And sleep beside their shields. That we despatch Amid the foe some voluntary spy, Is my advice

s: Rhesus be son of the tuneful Muse (and Thracian Strymon’s stream)
q: Son of the tuneful Muse, And Thracian Strymon’s stream

s: Hector is a lord of Troy
q: Thou brave descendant of a noble sire, Lord of this realm, O Hector

s: Hector defends Troy (against the Greek siege)
q: For this is the tenth year since thou hast waged An ineffectual war

s: Hector wage an ineffectual war (for ten years)
q: For this is the tenth year since thou hast waged An ineffectual war

s: Hector raised Rhesus (to the throne)
q: I raised you to the wide-extended throne

s: Hector lay siege to the turrets (reared by Greece)
q: to the turrets reared By Greece, thou now lay’st siege
